title: Energy available at each trophic level of a grassland

stimulus.title: A grassland food web with energy values
stimulus.text: The model shows part of a grassland food web. Each box gives the energy stored in new biomass at that population each year, in kJ per m² per year. Arrows point from the food to the organism that eats it. Hawks and mice are endotherms; grasshoppers, frogs and snakes are ectotherms.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the percentage of the energy stored by the grasshoppers that is stored by the frogs. Show your work.

rubric.point: Calculates 60 ÷ 720 × 100 = 8.3% (accept 8% or 8.33%), with the setup shown.

parts.sample: 60 ÷ 720 × 100 = 8.3% of the energy stored by the grasshoppers ends up stored by the frogs.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why the energy stored by the frogs is so much less than the energy stored by the grasshoppers.

rubric.point: Explains that most of the energy in grasshoppers is released as heat by the grasshoppers' (and frogs') cellular respiration or is not eaten or not digested (lost in feces, to decomposers), so only a small fraction becomes frog tissue.
accept: most energy is used in cellular respiration and lost as heat
not all grasshoppers are eaten, and some of what is eaten is not digested and leaves as feces
energy is used for movement and metabolism and released as heat, so little is stored as new biomass

parts.sample: Many grasshoppers are never eaten by frogs and pass to decomposers, and part of what frogs eat is not digested. Of the energy the frogs absorb, most is used in cellular respiration to power their bodies and is released as heat, so only about 8% is stored in new frog tissue.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A disease kills most of the mice. Predict how the frog population will change over the next year, and justify your prediction using the model.

rubric.point: Predicts a change in the frog population with a justification that follows the links in the model. Expected: frogs decrease, because snakes, having lost the mice as food, eat more frogs. Also accept: frogs eventually increase, if justified by the snake population falling (fewer mice to eat, and hawks, also short of mice, eating more snakes).
accept: frogs decrease because snakes switch to eating more frogs
frogs decline: with fewer mice, frogs become a larger share of the snakes' diet
more pressure on frogs from snakes, so fewer frogs
frogs may later increase because snakes decline when both snakes and hawks lose the mice

parts.sample: The frog population will decrease. In the model, snakes eat both mice and frogs. With most mice gone, the snakes will catch and eat more frogs, so more frogs die.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: The hawks store 1.2 kJ per m² per year, about 0.7% of the 178 kJ stored by the snakes and mice they eat. Predict the energy the hawks could store if they ate only snakes, keeping the same 0.7%, and justify your prediction using the trophic levels in the model.

rubric.point: Predicts that hawk storage falls to about 0.13 kJ per m² per year (0.007 × 18; accept about 0.1, or about a tenth of the present value), and justifies it: snakes store far less energy (18 kJ) than mice (160 kJ) because snakes feed a trophic level higher, so less energy is available to hawks.
accept: about 0.12-0.13 kJ, because 0.7% of 18 kJ is about 0.13
it drops to roughly one tenth, since snakes hold only 18 of the 178 kJ
less energy, because snakes are one trophic level above mice and store much less energy

parts.sample: About 0.007 × 18 = 0.13 kJ per m² per year, roughly a tenth of what the hawks store now. Mice eat grass, so they are primary consumers and store 160 kJ; snakes are a trophic level higher and store only 18 kJ, because energy is lost as heat at each extra step. Feeding only on snakes would leave the hawks with far less energy, so the hawk population would be much smaller.
